entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Helgaud (Helgaldus) was a Benedictine monk of the abbey of Fleury (Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire) in the early eleventh century and the author of the Epitoma vitae regis Rotberti pii, a hagiographic biography of King Robert II the Pious of France (r. 996–1031). Writing from one of the realm’s great monasteries, Helgaud portrayed Robert as a sacral, charitable, miracle-working king rather than as a purely political Capetian operator—an image that served monastic ideals of righteous rulership.

As a source, Helgaud is indispensable and problematic: he preserves unique anecdotes about Robert’s piety, marriages, and court, yet filters them through Fleury’s interests and hagiographic convention. Historians of the early Capetians depend on him alongside richer narrative sources to reconstruct the religious self-presentation of West Frankish kingship around the year 1000. Helgaud thus stands at the meeting point of monastic historiography and Capetian legitimacy.
